\chapter{Days of the Week}
\label{ch:te-days-of-the-week}
\hlchaptermodality{10}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name any day of the week in Telugu, including the Sunday that is counted rather than named for a planet.}

Run Somavāram through Śanivāram, then name Sunday \te{ఆదివారం}, \textquotedblleft{}the first day\textquotedblright{} — positional like Arabic's numbered days, not planetary.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[Somavāram Maṅgaḷavāram Budhavāram …]{\te{సోమవారం} to \te{ఆదివారం} — Telugu's week, with a twist on Sunday}

\label{lesson:TE-C10-vaaram}



\begin{quote}
Like Kannada, Telugu's week runs on Sanskrit deity-names — but its Sunday breaks the \textquotedblleft{}planet\textquotedblright{} pattern entirely, in a way even Kannada's doesn't.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Telugu} & \textbf{deity/planet} & \textbf{day} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\te{సోమవారం}} (\emph{Somavāram}) & \textbf{Moon} (Soma) & Monday \\
\textbf{\te{మంగళవారం}} (\emph{Maṅgaḷavāram}) & \textbf{Mars} (Maṅgala) & Tuesday \\
\textbf{\te{బుధవారం}} (\emph{Budhavāram}) & \textbf{Mercury} (Budha) & Wednesday \\
\textbf{\te{గురువారం}} (\emph{Guruvāram}) & \textbf{Jupiter} (Guru/Bṛhaspati) & Thursday \\
\textbf{\te{శుక్రవారం}} (\emph{Śukravāram}) & \textbf{Venus} (Śukra) & Friday \\
\textbf{\te{శనివారం}} (\emph{Śanivāram}) & \textbf{Saturn} (Śani) & Saturday \\
\textbf{\te{ఆదివారం}} (\emph{Ādivāram}) & — not a planet at all & Sunday \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
Five days match the familiar planet-deity pattern — but \textbf{\te{ఆదివారం}} (\emph{Ādivāram}) doesn't name the Sun at all. \textbf{\te{ఆది}} (\emph{ādi}) is Sanskrit for \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{the beginning, the first}.\textquotedblright{} So Telugu's Sunday literally means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{the first day}\textquotedblright{} — a \textbf{positional} name, like Arabic's numbered weekdays, sitting right next to six planet-names that don't work that way. Even within one single week, a language can mix completely different naming strategies.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Somavāram, Maṅgaḷavāram, Budhavāram, Guruvāram, Śukravāram, Śanivāram\textquotedblright{} — Monday through Saturday
  \item the odd one — \textquotedblleft{}Ādivāram\textquotedblright{} — not a planet, \textquotedblleft{}the first day\textquotedblright{}
  \item the parallel — like Arabic's numbered days, one Telugu day is positional too
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\te{ఆదివారం}} literally mean, and is it a planet-name? (\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}The first day\textquotedblright{}} — \textbf{ādi} \textquotedblleft{}beginning\textquotedblright{} — \textbf{not} a planet-name, unlike the other six.) What ending do the other six Telugu weekdays share? (\textbf{‑\te{వారం}} \emph{-vāram}, Sanskrit \textquotedblleft{}day,\textquotedblright{} each paired with a planet-deity.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[śa]{\te{శ} — the third s, and the last one}

\label{lesson:TE-S159-letter-sha}



\begin{quote}
You have two s-shapes already: \te{స}, and the curled one you met beside it. Say which of the two puts your tongue further back.

Two of the day names you have just learned carry a third one.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \te{శ}}
\textbf{\te{శ}} — \emph{śa}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{ś}, it is \textbf{śa}.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\te{శుక్రవారం}} \emph{śukravāram} — Friday
  \item \textbf{\te{శనివారం}} \emph{śanivāram} — Saturday
\end{itemize}

Both open on today's character. \textbf{The two ends of the week you have just recited begin with a letter you could not yet read.}

Now you have the whole set:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{letter} & \textbf{romanized} & \textbf{where the tongue goes} \\
\midrule
\te{స} & \emph{sa} & tip behind the teeth \\
\te{ష} & \emph{ṣa} & curled back along the roof \\
\te{శ} & \emph{śa} & flat against the front of the roof \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Telugu, Kannada and Hindi keep all three apart on the page. Tamil's own alphabet has none of them and adds borrowed shapes for Sanskrit words — same family, opposite decision.

\subsection*{Writing: \te{శ} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \te{శ} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed. Then write \te{స} and \te{ష} beside it.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at the two day names below and find \te{శ} at the front of each
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\te{శుక్రవారం}  ·  \te{శనివారం}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \te{శ} three times, saying \emph{śa} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} at \te{సంతోషం} and say which two of the three s letters are in it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \te{శ}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{śa}}.) Which two days of the week begin with it? (\textbf{\te{శుక్రవారం}} and \textbf{\te{శనివారం}}.) How many separate s letters does Telugu print? (\textbf{Three} — \te{స}, \te{ష}, \te{శ}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la]{\te{ల} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:TE-S114-letter-la}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \te{ఇ} — what does it do? And one from further back: \te{య}?

One character this time — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \te{ల}}
\textbf{\te{ల}} — \emph{la}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{l}, it is \textbf{la}.

You already say these, and every one of them has \te{ల} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\te{ధన్యవాదములు}} \emph{dhanyavādamulu} — thank you (dhanyavādamulu — \textquotedblleft{}utterances of 'worthy'\textquotedblright{})
  \item \textbf{\te{లేదు}} \emph{lēdu} — no / there isn't (lēdu)
  \item \textbf{\te{పరవాలేదు}} \emph{paravālēdu} — it's okay / no problem / you're welcome
  \item \textbf{\te{రేపు} \te{కలుద్దాం}} \emph{rēpu kaluddām} — see you tomorrow
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \te{ల} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \te{ల} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \te{ల} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\te{ధన్యవాదములు}  ·  \te{లేదు}  ·  \te{నమస్కారం}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \te{ల} three times, saying \emph{la} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \te{ల} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \te{ల}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{la}}.) Name one word you already say that contains it.

One more, from much earlier: \te{ప} — what does it do?
\end{tcolorbox}
